newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's first task: who stays, who goes?.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's first task: who stays, who goes?.

text.p: If President Bill Clinton wins re-election, his first task will be to decide who's in and who's out of the Cabinet and the White House staff.
As he learned in 1992, it is not an easy process.

Four years ago Clinton made some disastrous appointments, naming lawyer Zoe Baird attorney general only to withdraw her nomination as the nation's top law enforcement officer because she had not paid Social Security taxes for her nanny.

"When you look at what we did at the end of 1992, it is obvious that mistakes were made. We didn't have a clue about what we were doing. We didn't even know what we didn't know," said one White House official.
"This is our last, best chance to get it right," he added.
Intent on avoiding the mistakes of the past, Clinton has already devised a system to fill the spots that are expected to open up as people leave, or are given the boot, if he wins.
On the outside, Vernon Jordan, a longtime Washington powerbroker, and former White House deputy chief of staff Erskine Bowles have been tapped to lead the transition.

On the inside, a senior White House source said chief of staff Leon Panetta was taking the lead on how the Cabinet may be reshuffled while Evelyn Lieberman, one of his two deputies, was studying the key White House jobs.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said no decisions have yet been made, despite all the speculation: "Nobody has had the conversation that counts, and that's with the president."
Here is a look at how some of the main jobs may change.
Chief of Staff

Panetta's first job may be to find a replacement for himself as chief of staff, the most powerful job in the White House next to the president. Officials say it is a common assumption Panetta will leave, possibly to run for California governor.
But several said the widely respected Panetta has promised an orderly transition, suggesting he may not leave quickly.

Clinton learned the sensitivity of the job the hard way, replacing his first chief of staff, childhood friend Thomas "Mack" McClarty, with Panetta after 18 months when the native Arkansan's lack of Washington expertise became a liability.

A host of names circulate to replace Panetta, including: Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor, deputy chief of staff Harold Ickes and Bowles. Sometimes cited as dark horses for the job are White House Counsel Jack Quinn, a former chief of staff to Vice President Al Gore, as well as Lieberman.
Secretary of State
The conventional wisdom is that Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who turned 71 on Sunday, wants to leave public service after the grueling travel he has endured for four years.
But one senior official said that rumors of his imminent departure may be exaggerated: "I am not convinced that a lot of the speculation about Christopher will prove right."
His job, the most prestigious in the Cabinet, is also among the most sought after.
Potential successors include former Sen. George Mitchell, former Assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke and United Nations Ambassador Madeleine Albright.
Others include Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, Kantor and retiring Sen. Sam Nunn, the Georgian with a history of antagonizing presidents by speaking his mind.
Secetary of Defense
Defense Secretary William Perry, 69, has said he will not decide on retiring until after the election, but speaking two weeks ago he did not sound desperate to hang on to his job.
"It was not something I sought, something I was anxious to do," he told reporters. "It was something which was urged on me and after a lot of consideration I finally decided to do."
John Deutch, the director of the Central Intelligence Agency, is widely expected to move to Defense if Perry goes.
Secretary of the Treasury

Several White House officials said Rubin is expected to keep his job, saying he enjoys the position, seems perfectly suited to it and enjoys unrivaled access to the White House, where he attends the daily senior staff meeting at 7:30 a.m.
Attorney General

At the Justice Department, Janet Reno is seen as one of the more vulnerable members of the Cabinet. A month ago, Reno suggested she would like to be re-appointed, telling reporters she would "be honored and ... would look forward to it."
But several White House officials said she may well be elbowed aside, for example if Kantor were to want her job.
